extracted.intended_audience: reviewers (and authors) for ACL 2023; especially novice conference reviewers in NLP
extracted.subtask_description: Practical tutorial and policy guidance for writing and managing peer reviews for ACL'23 conference submissions, covering pre-assignment checks, reading strategy, what to write, discussion/response, and ACL23-specific policies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Confidentiality of submission materials
rubrics_metrics.description: All information about submissions and reviews that you receive as part of your assignment is confidential.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not discuss individual papers on social media or elsewhere in ways that could identify submissions or reveal your reviewer identity; if commenting publicly, keep examples general and anonymized.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide accurate reviewer profile information
rubrics_metrics.description: Ensure you have provided all information requested by the venue (sign-up forms, reviewer profiles like Semantic Scholar) used for computing conflicts and assignments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Update your Semantic Scholar/global profile as instructed (ACL site path provided) so automatic matching places you on appropriate papers; inaccurate profiles reduce match quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Qualification check before accepting assignment
rubrics_metrics.description: Skim an assigned paper to decide whether you are sufficiently qualified to review it, especially for core methodology.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It is acceptable to review somewhat outside your subfield if you know the core methodology; if expertise lacks for certain aspects, state that explicitly in the review and use the confidence-score field. For very novel/atypical papers you may be asked to review despite imperfect match.

rubrics_metrics.name: Check for conflicts of interest (anonymity/personal/academic)
rubrics_metrics.description: When assigned a paper, check whether you know or can guess the authors and whether you have academic or personal conflicts that warrant recusal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If anonymity is compromised, contact the chair/SAC/AC and the paper may be desk-rejected; if you personally know the authors or will collaborate, request re-assignment. For submissions obviously too close to your own imminent submission, recuse and inform senior area chair.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anonymity handling and disclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: If the review process is anonymous but you learn the authors' identities (e.g., famous paper or guessed identity), indicate your awareness of the authors’ identity in the review form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If anonymity is not preserved in the submission itself (authors failed to anonymize), contact AC/SAC about desk-rejection; be cautious about discovering identities via references or preprints and avoid letting that bias the review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Desk-rejection triggers (format/policy violations)
rubrics_metrics.description: Papers that do not preserve anonymity, ignore style guides, or exceed page limits (page limit excludes the ethical considerations section) can be flagged for desk-rejection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report such violations to the area chair/action editor rather than just penalizing in your review; indicate policy violations in the rebuttal if you are an author.

rubrics_metrics.name: Time management for reviews
rubrics_metrics.description: Block time in your calendar to perform the review and submit it on time, preferably a few days before the deadline.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Estimate time based on reading in-depth and writing/editing; avoid doing reviewing in a single session—write a draft then revisit it after letting impressions settle to avoid knee-jerk reactions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid commenting on first skim; read strategically
rubrics_metrics.description: Don't annotate/comment extensively during the first read; first understand the paper type and contribution before detailed criticism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Skim to determine type (experimental, resource, analysis, reproduction, survey, short vs long). For experimental papers, read intro and methods first and delay looking at results until you’ve judged whether the approach would answer the posed question.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate the paper appropriate to its type and length
rubrics_metrics.description: Adjust expectations depending on paper type (experimental vs resource vs analysis vs reproduction vs survey) and length (long vs short).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Long papers should contain thorough evaluation and analysis; short papers may provide proof-of-concept or an interesting finding and need only minimal but convincing evidence. Judge each paper for what it is, not by a prototypical paper in your subfield.

rubrics_metrics.name: Focus on clarity of research question and methodology
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess whether the research question is clear, the methods are described sufficiently to answer it, and whether the approach plausibly addresses the question.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When reading, pause to ask: is the research question clear? Do I believe the method answers it? Do I care about the answer? Will it advance the field? Only then evaluate results; a negative result can be a valid contribution if the study is sound.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be explicit about limitations in your expertise
rubrics_metrics.description: If your expertise does not cover certain aspects of the submission, explicitly state that in your review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Indicate which parts you are not qualified to judge and use the confidence score; this helps area chairs weigh your input appropriately.

rubrics_metrics.name: Actionable, specific feedback for authors
rubrics_metrics.description: Give concrete, actionable suggestions rather than vague criticisms (e.g., instead of 'not enough experiments', suggest a specific dataset or validation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make sure authors have a clear path forward: specific datasets, analyses, or corrections. If something could be fixed easily in camera-ready, state how; if missing analyses are central to the claim label them weaknesses rather than suggestions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Write reviews for multiple audiences (authors, reviewers, AC/SAC)
rubrics_metrics.description: Structure the review so it is useful to the authors, stimulates helpful discussion with other reviewers, and enables AC/SAC to decide without having to read the paper in full.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors need actionable guidance; other reviewers need entry points for discussion (explicitly contrast when useful); AC/SAC need self-contained, specific summaries to aid meta-review and calibration across the area.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make reviews self-contained for area chairs
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide enough detail and specificity in your review so the area chair can write a metareview without re-reading the paper deeply.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Summarize key strengths and weaknesses, evidence supporting them, and how damaging each weakness is to the central claim; avoid only high-level statements without supporting detail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Participation in the discussion period
rubrics_metrics.description: Engage in post-review discussion if invited, especially when there is variation in scores.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the discussion to catch mistakes, misunderstandings, or policy violations; update your review to reflect new information that arises during discussion so authors see accurate feedback.

rubrics_metrics.name: Author response handling and purpose
rubrics_metrics.description: The author response period is primarily for clarifying misunderstandings and indicating how easy-to-make changes will be addressed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the reviewer misunderstood something present in the paper, authors should point to where it is stated. If reviewers asked for reframing or minor changes possible in camera-ready, authors should explain how they'll address them. Per ACL'23, authors may not report new experimental results performed after submission.

rubrics_metrics.name: Policy on reporting post-submission experiments (ACL'23)
rubrics_metrics.description: ACL'23 disallows reporting experimental results that were not part of the original submission in the author response.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When authors mention results performed since submission, reviewers should consider whether those results are necessary to back claims (then missing results are a weakness) or merely nice-to-have (then a suggestion).

rubrics_metrics.name: Flagging policy violations in rebuttal
rubrics_metrics.description: If a reviewer receives or authors identify a review that violates conference policies, flag it in the rebuttal form for meta-reviewer consideration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors should explicitly point out policy violations; reviewers and chairs will take violations into account during meta-review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cautious lookup of references to avoid de-anonymization
rubrics_metrics.description: Looking up references or concurrent work while reviewing can reveal the authors' identities via non-anonymous preprints.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do such lookups cautiously; if you discover identities, note that awareness in the review and be mindful of biases it may introduce.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recuse from reviewing when work is too close to your own
rubrics_metrics.description: If the submission looks very close to your own work that is about to be submitted, recuse yourself from reviewing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contact your senior area chair; don't attempt to review work that would present an academic conflict.

rubrics_metrics.name: Report reviewer confidence and limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the review form’s confidence score and annotate parts of the review where you are less confident.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Confidence scores help chairs interpret reviews from novice vs experienced reviewers and indicate where further calibration or another reviewer may be needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain professional and constructive tone
rubrics_metrics.description: Be respectful and avoid harsh language in reviews.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Constructive tone improves usefulness; see linked resources on avoiding harsh language. Even when critical, thank reviewers and be professional—authors are colleagues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use reviews to spark reviewer discussion
rubrics_metrics.description: It is acceptable and often useful to open a door for discussion on particular topics in your review to interact with other reviewers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: You can explicitly disagree with other reviewers (e.g., 'unlike Reviewer 2, I...') but remain professional and use the discussion period for deeper exchange.
